# Nehemiah Chapter 6 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 471v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/NEH_006_page_001.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** When Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arab, and the rest of our enemies heard that I had rebuilt the wall and that no breach remained in it — though up to that time I had not yet set the doors in the gates —

**2** Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, "Come, let us meet together in one of the villages on the plain of Ono." But they were planning to do me harm.

**3** I sent messengers to them, saying, "I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to come down to you?"

**4** They sent to me four times in this manner, and I answered them the same way.

**5** Then Sanballat sent his servant to me a fifth time with an open letter in his hand.

**6** In it was written: "It is reported among the nations — and Geshem confirms it — that you and the Jews are planning to rebel. That is why you are building the wall. And according to these reports, you intend to become their king.

**7** You have also appointed prophets to proclaim concerning you in Jerusalem: 'There is a king in Judah!' Now these reports will reach the king. So come, let us take counsel together."

**8** I sent to him, saying, "Nothing like what you are saying has taken place. You are inventing it from your own mind."

**9** For they were all trying to frighten us, thinking, "Their hands will grow weak and drop from the work, and it will not be done." Now strengthen my hands, O God.

**10** I went to the house of Shemaiah son of Delaiah son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his home. He said, "Let us meet in the house of God, inside the temple. Let us shut the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you — by night they are coming to kill you."

**11** But I said, "Should a man like me flee? And could someone like me go into the temple and live? I will not go."

**12** I perceived that God had not sent him, but that he had pronounced this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.

**13** He was hired for this purpose: that I should be afraid and act accordingly and sin, and they would have an evil report with which to reproach me.

**14** Remember, O my God, Tobiah and Sanballat for what they have done, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who tried to make me afraid.

**15** So the wall was completed on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days.

**16** When all our enemies heard of it and all the surrounding nations saw it, they fell greatly in their own esteem, for they recognized that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God.

**17** Moreover, in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah's letters came to them.

**18** For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah, and his son Jehohanan had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah.

**19** They also spoke of his good deeds in my presence and reported my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to intimidate me.

---

## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Nehemiah 6 presents the climactic phase of opposition — and the climactic moment of completion. The chapter narrates three increasingly cunning strategies: repeated invitations to a meeting (diplomatic trap, vv. 1-4), an open letter of accusation (public smear, vv. 5-9), and a hired false prophet urging Nehemiah to violate Torah by hiding in the sanctuary (spiritual manipulation, vv. 10-13). Nehemiah's discernment in each case demonstrates that faithfulness requires not only courage but wisdom. The wall's completion in fifty-two days (v. 15) is the narrative's theological crescendo, acknowledged even by Israel's enemies as evidence of divine action (v. 16). The chapter closes with a troubling coda: Tobiah's deep connections among Judah's nobility (vv. 17-19) foreshadow ongoing internal compromise.

---

## Disagreement Log

### V.3 — "great work" vs. "important project"
- **EMET:** "great work" (*melakhah gedolah*) / **LOGOS:** "great work" / **PNEUMA:** "important project"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "great work" — Literal rendering of *melakhah gedolah*. PNEUMA's "important project" diminishes the theological weight of *melakhah*, which echoes creation and tabernacle language.

### V.9 — prayer placement: "strengthen my hands" vs. "give me strength"
- **EMET:** "strengthen my-hands" / **LOGOS:** "O God, strengthen my hands" / **PNEUMA:** "God, give me strength"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Now strengthen my hands, O God" — Preserves the Hebrew body-part idiom (*chazzaq yadai*) while clarifying that this is a prayer. PNEUMA's generalization loses the specific image of hands engaged in building work.

### V.16 — "fell in their own esteem" vs. "were demoralized" vs. "were afraid"
- **EMET:** "fell greatly in-their-own-eyes" / **LOGOS:** "fell greatly in their own esteem" / **PNEUMA:** "were demoralized and deeply shaken"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "fell greatly in their own esteem" — The Hebrew *va-yippelu be-eyneyhem* means their self-confidence collapsed. LOGOS captures this precisely. PNEUMA adds interpretive expansion not in the text.

---

*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
